nota.en: Only in Spain. Recognize it; in Latin America say «ustedes».

texto.en: In Foundations you met the pronouns. Now let's see how they fit together. Spanish has two things English doesn't: gender in the plural (nosotros/nosotras, ellos/ellas) and a formal «you» (usted, and ustedes for groups). A group of women takes the feminine form (nosotras, ellas). If there's even one man in the group, use the masculine form (nosotros, ellos). There's no word for «it» as a subject: you simply use the verb, as in «Es de México» (It's / He's / She's from Mexico).
Tap each pronoun to hear it.

apoyo.en: informal; accent mark: tú = you, tu = your
polite; uses the same verb form as él and ella
accent mark: él = he, el = the
Latin America: for any group, friends or strangers

titulo.en: Vosotros: recognize it, don't worry about it

texto.en: In Spain, a group of friends is «vosotros» (or «vosotras» for women), and it has its own verb forms, such as «sois» and «estáis». In Latin America, ustedes is used for every group, friends or strangers, and that's what you'll use in this course. You'll see vosotros in the verb tables so you can recognize it in movies, books or on a trip to Spain.

titulo.en: Drop the pronoun (most of the time)

texto.en: The verb ending already tells you who: soy = I am, somos = we are. So Spanish speakers usually drop the pronoun: «Soy de Chicago», «Somos amigos». Keep it in three cases: 1) contrast: «Yo soy de Lima y él es de Quito»; 2) clarity, because él, ella and usted share the same verb form: «Ella es profesora»; 3) short answers and questions: «¿Quién es de México? —Yo.», «¿Y tú?». Usted is often kept to sound polite.
The pronoun in brackets is optional. Add it only for contrast or clarity.

titulo.en: Ser: what someone or something IS

texto.en: Ser is the «to be» for things that define someone: name and identity (Soy Tom), job (Es ingeniera), nationality and origin (Somos peruanos… Son de Perú), and personality or physical description (Eres muy simpático, Carlos es alto). Ser is irregular: its forms don't look like the infinitive, so learn the table by heart.
Every form is different. vosotros sois is only used in Spain.
Masculine forms ending in -o change to -a. Forms ending in a consonant add -a (and lose the accent mark). Forms ending in -e stay the same.

Spanish writes nationalities with a small letter: Soy mexicana, not «Mexicana». Countries keep their capital letter: México, Perú. Descriptive words agree with the person too: Carlos es alto, Ana es alta. Words ending in -e or a consonant, like inteligente and joven, have one form for everybody. To check something, add ¿no? at the end: Eres de Perú, ¿no?

titulo.en: Gender and articles: el, la, un, una

objetivo.en: Know whether a noun is masculine or feminine, use el, la, un and una correctly, and make the adjective agree.

nota.en: Latin America. In Spain: el ordenador.
Masculine, even though it ends in -a.
Masculine, even though it ends in -a.
Feminine, even though it ends in -o.

explicacion.en: día ends in -a but it's masculine: el día, buenos días.
mano ends in -o but it's feminine: la mano.
casa is feminine, so the adjective is feminine too: nueva.

texto.en: In Spanish every noun is masculine or feminine, even things: el libro (the book) is masculine, la mesa (the table) is feminine. The gender is grammar, not meaning, so a chair isn't «female» in any real sense. Good news: most nouns ending in -o are masculine and most ending in -a are feminine. Words ending in -dad are feminine (la ciudad). For other endings (el café, la llave, el hotel) learn the article with the word, like a package: never learn «mesa», learn «la mesa».
The article must match the noun's gender.

titulo.en: Learn each noun with its article

texto.en: A few common words break the pattern: el día and el mapa are masculine; la mano and la foto are feminine. For people, the article shows the gender: el profesor / la profesora, el estudiante / la estudiante (same word, different article). Remember: after ser, jobs go without un/una (Soy profesora), and don't mix up el (the) with él (he). Adjectives go after the noun and agree: un carro nuevo, una casa nueva.

objetivo.en: Make nouns plural, use los, las, unos and unas, and make every word in the phrase agree in gender and number.

nota.en: Same form for masculine and feminine.
Same form for masculine and feminine.

explicacion.en: The adjective agrees in gender AND number: casas is feminine plural → bonitas.

texto.en: Plurals are easy. If the noun ends in a vowel, add -s: libro → libros, café → cafés. If it ends in a consonant, add -es: ciudad → ciudades, hotel → hoteles. If it ends in -z, change it to c and add -es: lápiz → lápices. Sometimes an accent mark appears or disappears to keep the stress in the same place: joven → jóvenes, inglés → ingleses. The article changes too: el → los, la → las, un → unos, una → unas (unos/unas = some).

apoyo.en: consonant → + es (the accent stays on í)

titulo.en: Adjectives agree in gender and number

texto.en: Adjectives follow the noun and copy its gender and number.

In a Spanish phrase, the article, the noun and the adjective all match: el carro rojo, la casa roja, los carros rojos, las casas rojas. Mixed groups take the masculine plural: los estudiantes can be all men or men and women; las estudiantes are only women. The same goes for los hermanos (brothers, or brothers and sisters) and mis amigos. Possessives have plurals too: mi amigo → mis amigos, tu llave → tus llaves.

titulo.en: Estar: feelings, places, and ser or estar

objetivo.en: Use all forms of estar to say how people feel and where people and things are, and choose between ser and estar.

nota.en: Same form for men and women.

explicacion.en: Where someone is → estar.
Where you're from is part of who you are → ser.
The adjective agrees with Ana y Lucía, two women: feminine plural → cansadas.

texto.en: Estar is the «to be» for states and places: how someone feels right now (Estoy cansada, Estamos contentos) and where someone or something is (Estoy en el trabajo, El baño está aquí). Notice the accent marks: estás, está, están. Estar is irregular only in yo (estoy) and in where the stress falls.
vosotros estáis is only used in Spain.

Ask yourself: is it what someone IS (identity, origin, job, personality) or how or where they are right now? «Soy de Lima» (origin: ser) but «Estoy en Quito» (location: estar). «Carlos es alto» (description: ser) but «Carlos está cansado» (state: estar). A rhyme helps: «How you feel and where you are, that's when you use estar.»

objetivo.en: Use all forms of tener to talk about family and things you have, count from 0 to 100, and ask and say someone's age.

nota.en: Tengo veinte años = I'm twenty (literally «I have twenty years»).

titulo.en: Tener: to have… and to be (years old)

texto.en: Tener means «to have»: Tengo un gato (I have a cat), Tenemos dos hijos (We have two children). Spanish also uses it for age: Tengo veinte años = I'm twenty, literally «I have twenty years». To ask: ¿Cuántos años tienes? (tú) or ¿Cuántos años tiene usted? Tener is irregular: yo tengo, and the e becomes ie in tienes, tiene, tienen.
The -ie- forms are in the middle; nosotros keeps the plain e: tenemos.
Each of these has its own word.
16–19 = «ten and six…» (dieci-), 21–29 = «twenty and one…» (veinti-). Watch the accent marks.
From 31, write three words: treinta y uno, cuarenta y cinco. 100 is cien.

cuántos and cuántas agree with the noun they ask about: ¿Cuántos hermanos tienes? (masculine) / ¿Cuántas hermanas tienes? (feminine). Before a masculine noun, uno becomes un: un año, veintiún años, treinta y un años. You'll also see numbers in phone numbers, said digit by digit or in pairs: cero, nueve, ocho…

objetivo.en: Conjugate regular -ar, -er and -ir verbs in the present (hablar, trabajar, estudiar, comer, beber, vivir) to talk about your languages, work, studies and daily habits.

nota.en: In Latin America you'll also hear «tomar» for drinks.
Hablo un poco de español = I speak a little Spanish.
With an accent mark: té = tea, te = you (object).

explicacion.en: With yo the ending is always -o: hablo, como, vivo.
-ir verbs use -imos with nosotros: vivimos. -emos is for -er verbs: comemos.
Languages are written with a small letter in Spanish.

texto.en: Every Spanish verb ends in -ar, -er or -ir: hablar, comer, vivir. To use it, take off the ending and add a new one for each person: habl-ar → habl-o (I speak). English only adds -s for «he/she»; Spanish has a different ending for every person, and that's why you can drop the pronoun. The present covers «I speak», «I'm speaking» and «I do speak».
Endings: -o, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an.
-er endings: -o, -es, -e, -emos, -éis, -en. -ir endings are the same except -imos and -ís.

-er and -ir verbs are twins: they only differ with nosotros (comemos / vivimos) and vosotros. The yo form always ends in -o. Languages take a small letter: hablo inglés, estudio español. Use «un poco de» for «a little»: Hablo un poco de francés. Careful: trabajo is also a noun: el trabajo = work, the job.

objetivo.en: Make any sentence negative with no, and ask and answer questions with qué, quién, dónde, cómo, cuántos/as, cuál and por qué.

nota.en: ¿Cuál es tu número de teléfono? = What's your phone number?
Two words and an accent mark.
Always feminine: la persona, even for a man.
Before the verb, with no «no»: Nunca bebo café.

explicacion.en: no always goes right before the verb.
To ask for a piece of information (a number, a name, an address) use ¿cuál es…?, not ¿qué es…?
Question words always carry an accent mark: ¿dónde?, ¿qué?, ¿cómo?

titulo.en: No: one word, before the verb

texto.en: To make any sentence negative, put no right before the verb. There's no «do/don't» in Spanish: No hablo francés (I don't speak French), No trabajo hoy (I'm not working today), No tengo carro (I don't have a car). When you answer a question, you often hear no twice: «¿Vives aquí? —No, no vivo aquí» (No, I don't live here). nunca (never) also goes before the verb, without no: Nunca bebo café.
They always carry an accent mark and go at the start of the question.

Put the question word first, then the verb, then the subject if you need it: ¿Dónde vive Ana? ¿Qué estudia Carlos? A yes/no question can keep the order of a statement; only your voice rises at the end: ¿Hablas inglés? You can also put the verb first: ¿Habla usted inglés? To ask for a name, number or address, use ¿cuál es…?: ¿Cuál es tu número de teléfono? Answer ¿por qué? with porque (one word): Porque trabajo en México.

explicacion.en: Age → tener.
usted takes the él/ella form of the verb: vive, not vives.

texto.en: A complete introduction has six parts: your name (Me llamo…), where you're from (Soy de… / Soy + nationality), where you live (Vivo en…), your age (Tengo … años), your job or studies (Soy enfermera / Trabajo como mesero / Estudio…) and your languages (Hablo…). Remember the three «to be» traps: ser for nationality and job, estar for how and where you are, tener for age. With usted, every verb takes the él/ella form: ¿Dónde vive usted?
A model introduction, one part per sentence:

ejemplos.texto: Soy mexicana, pero vivo en Chicago.

traduccion.en: I'm Mexican, but I live in Chicago.

ejemplos.texto: Trabajo como enfermera en un hospital.

traduccion.en: I work as a nurse in a hospital.

ejemplos.texto: Hablo español, inglés y un poco de francés.

traduccion.en: I speak Spanish, English and a little French.

ejemplos.texto: Tengo un perro y no tengo hijos.

traduccion.en: I have a dog and I don't have children.
